K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM}: Control-Oriented Structured Bilinear World Models under Partial Observation

Santosh M. Rajkumar ††thanks: Department of Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering (in Columbus, OH, USA) (E-mail: {rajkumar.36, goswami.78}@osu.edu ) Affiliation: The Ohio State University    Sriram Narayanan ††thanks: Department of Mechanical, Materials, and Aerospace Engineering (in Morgantown, WV, USA) (E-mail: sriram.narayanan@mail.wvu.edu) Affiliation: West Virginia University    Samuel E. Otto ††thanks: Sibley School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering (in Ithaca, NY, USA) (E-mail: s.otto@cornell.edu)
   Affiliation: Cornell University    Debdipta Goswami11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: The Ohio State University
Abstract

World models learn internal simulators of environment dynamics for prediction, planning, and control, yet learning them from limited, noisy, and partial observations remains challenging. While much progress has focused on pixel-based observations, many physical systems instead provide vector-valued measurements that reveal only part of the underlying state. We introduce K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM}, a probabilistic world model for prediction and control under partial observation. K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} couples Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics with a nonlinear observation decoder and performs probabilistic latent-state inference through the learned model via extended Kalman filtering and smoothing, without a separately trained inference network. Its bilinear structure enables exact propagation of the maintained Gaussian belief through the latent transition and efficient rollouts for uncertainty-aware model predictive path integral (MPPI) control. For training K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM}, we present a generalized expectation conditional maximization (GECM) procedure with closed-form updates for the generators, noise covariances, and latent prior, complemented by gradient-based decoder learning. A Koopman-consistent initialization selects the latent dimension from data and initializes the action-dependent dynamics. With limited training data, K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} achieves lower long-horizon prediction error than the evaluated baselines on partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems, while substantially reducing training time relative to the strongest prediction baseline. On high-dimensional MuJoCo Menagerie robots, it achieves competitive tracking accuracy with low per-step computation times, demonstrating potential for real-time deployment. These results support structured probabilistic dynamics as a data- and compute-efficient approach to world modeling and control under partial observation.

1 Introduction

Physical AI systems, such as robots and other embodied agents, must infer environmental dynamics from noisy, partial observations and anticipate the consequences of their actions [1]. Although physics-based models and system identification underpin prediction and control, modeling complex, contact-rich, and unstructured environments remains challenging, and large-scale models can impose substantial computational demands [1, 2, 3]. World models (WMs) learn compact, predictive representations of environmental dynamics, supporting forward prediction and counterfactual rollouts for decision-making [4, 5]. Unlike model-free RL (MFRL), which learns policies or value functions without explicitly modeling dynamics, WMs predict action outcomes to support model predictive control (MPC) and model-based RL (MBRL) [6, 7]. Compared with MFRL, WMs can reduce costly interactions with physical systems by enabling planning and learning through imagined rollouts [8].

However, learning reliable WMs from noisy, partial observations remains challenging in real-world robotics [9, 10, 11]. Partial observation affects both pixel- and vector-based settings [12, 13], as sensor measurements often reveal only a subset of the underlying state [14, 15, 16]. For example, a mobile robot may observe its position without directly measuring its velocity. The resulting observation sequences can be non-Markovian even when the underlying dynamics are Markovian, motivating probabilistic latent-state inference to maintain a belief over hidden states and propagate uncertainty through time.

Existing WM learning methods often require substantial action-labeled data [17, 12], posing challenges for learning directly from limited environmental interactions. A common approach is to learn models in simulation and subsequently adapt them to the target environment; however, data-efficient adaptation to changing environments remains challenging [8]. These challenges motivate methods that can learn WMs directly from limited interaction data. Parametric state-space models (SSMs) that incorporate dynamical or physical structure offer a promising approach to improving data efficiency and generalization while supporting reliable continuous control [18, 19]. Moreover, interpretable latent dynamics can facilitate failure diagnosis and monitoring of robotic systems during deployment [20]. Together, these considerations motivate investigating structured parametric SSMs for data-efficient and interpretable world modeling.

Real-world robotic tasks subject to actuator limits and environmental constraints often require rapid and continuous control updates, motivating the use of real-time MPC [21, 22, 23]. MPC is also used in MBRL to select actions by optimizing action sequences online in the latent space of learned WMs [24, 25]. However, the high-dimensional action spaces of complex robotic systems can make online planning computationally demanding, limiting scalability and real-time deployment [26, 27]. This limitation is further exacerbated in WMs that use densely connected neural networks [20]. Introducing control-oriented dynamical structure into latent transitions can facilitate efficient predictive control, as illustrated by locally linear SSMs [28, 29]. This motivates the development of control-oriented WMs whose structured latent transitions enable efficient planning for real-time deployment.

In this work, we develop K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM}, a Koopman bilinear-structured Probabilistic World Model for prediction and downstream control of partially observed systems with vector-valued measurements. Our key contributions are: i) Probabilistic world modeling with structured latent dynamics and model-induced inference: we couple Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics with a nonlinear decoder and model-induced inference, without a separately trained inference network. Koopman coordinates are treated as latent random variables inferred through the observation likelihood rather than lifted from full-state measurements, and for fixed actions the linear-Gaussian transition propagates the maintained Gaussian belief exactly, with linearization confined to the decoder. ii) Structure-exploiting GECM learning: we derive closed-form conditional updates for the generators, noise covariances, and initial latent-state distribution, complemented by gradient-based nonlinear decoder learning. iii) Koopman-consistent initialization and dimension selection: we combine delay-coordinate representations with action-conditioned generator regression to initialize the latent dynamics and select the latent dimension from data. iv) Uncertainty-aware planning and empirical validation: we integrate K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} into an uncertainty-aware MPPI scheme and demonstrate improved prediction performance from limited data and reduced training time on partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems, alongside competitive tracking accuracy and computationally efficient control on four high-dimensional MuJoCo Menagerie robots.

1.1 Related Work

WMs with pixel-based observations.

Early pixel-based WMs include [30], where a VAE compresses images into latent codes and an RNN predicts latent dynamics. PlaNet learns latent dynamics for planning [31], while the Dreamer family trains policies through latent imagination, spanning continuous control [32], Atari with discrete latents [33], real-robot online learning [8], and scalable control across diverse domains [34]. Recent JEPA-style methods instead learn decoder-free predictive representations, often from images or videos, by predicting target embeddings rather than reconstructing pixels [4, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39]. World-model learning from large-scale videos and pretrained video models has been explored in [40] and [12], respectively. Although pixel-based world models are effective in visual domains, their representation-learning challenges differ from those arising with vector-valued observations [41]. The Dreamer family [33, 34] also supports vector-valued inputs, but its reported limitations on vector-based continuous-control tasks motivate WMs tailored to this setting [41].

Neural SSMs.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), including LSTMs [42] and GRUs [43], encode observation history in hidden states for sequence prediction. Kalman-style models, including Backprop KF [44], RKN [45], Ac-RKN [46], and HiP-RSSM [47], incorporate Gaussian filtering updates into neural architectures for latent-state estimation and dynamics prediction. Their evaluations primarily emphasize estimation and prediction, with less attention to task-level control and downstream decision-making. Variational autoencoder (VAE)-based control-oriented neural SSMs such as DVBF [48] jointly learn latent representations and dynamics, while NewtonianVAE [49] imposes explicit position–velocity structure to enable proportional control in latent space. However, partially conditioned amortized inference can introduce a conditioning gap that compromises learning of latent transition dynamics [50].

Linear and locally-linear SSMs.

MTS3 [51] is a prediction-oriented WM for vector-valued observations built on hierarchical linear Gaussian SSMs. Its slow-time-scale model uses aggregated action abstractions, which could complicate the translation of abstract plans into primitive actions. Control-oriented locally linear SSMs are developed in [28, 29], while [52] learns nonlinear latent transitions with curvature regularization to support locally linear control. However, local linear approximations may lose accuracy away from nominal trajectories and require repeated linearization during trajectory optimization.

Decoder-free WMs.

Decoder-free WMs such as TD-MPC [24], TD-MPC2 [25], and DCWM [41] learn models of latent transitions, rewards, and values without reconstructing observations, enabling online planning for continuous control. Their standard formulations do not explicitly maintain beliefs over hidden states, which may limit performance when observations or stacked histories provide insufficient state information. Moreover, online planning with densely connected neural models can incur substantial computational overhead, potentially limiting real-time deployment [20]. Fac-TDMPC [20] reduces planning latency through latent factorization and decentralized planning. However, its additive reward/value decomposition can inadequately capture dependencies among joint actions, and the authors report slower learning in some highly dynamic tasks requiring coordinated control.

Koopman operator-based methods.

Koopman operator theory offers a promising approach to structured world modeling through linear, bilinear, or semilinear evolution in latent space, potentially extending predictive validity across broader operating regimes [53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59]. However, dictionary selection and learning from partial observations remain important challenges [60]. Existing approaches include linear latent dynamics with learned dictionaries, as in DKUC [61], and bilinear dynamics with prespecified dictionaries [62, 63]. These formulations rely on full-state measurements, which may be unavailable in real-world robotics, and manually specified embedding dimensions, without explicit uncertainty quantification. Otto et al. [64] learn bilinear latent dynamics from partially observed trajectories without prespecifying a dictionary. However, their formulation assumes linearly independent observation functions and an affine decoder, which may limit its suitability for latent representations requiring nonlinear observation mappings, such as those derived for certain aerial robots in [58]. Latent-dimension selection also remains empirical.

2 K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM}: Koopman Bilinear-Structured Probabilistic World Model

In a partially observed setting, let x∈𝒳⊆ℝnx\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} denote the true but unobserved state of an embodied system, let a∈𝒜⊆ℝma\in\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} represent the control input (action), and let y∈𝒴⊆ℝnyy\in\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_{y}} denote the observation, which provides only partial information about the underlying state. We assume uniform sampling with interval Δ​t\Delta t, such that for all k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, the sampling instants are given by tk=k​Δ​tt_{k}=k\Delta t. The resulting discrete-time SSM of the system is given by

xk+1=Fd​(xk,ak),yk=g⁡(xk)+νk,νk∼𝒩⁡(0,Σν),\displaystyle x_{k+1}=F_{d}(x_{k},a_{k}),\qquad y_{k}=g(x_{k})+\nu_{k},\quad\nu_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{\nu}), (1)

where Fd:𝒳×𝒜→𝒳F_{d}\!:\!\mathcal{X}\!\times\!\mathcal{A}\!\to\!\mathcal{X} denotes the unknown discrete-time flow map induced by the underlying continuous-time dynamics x˙​(t)=F⁡(x⁡(t),a⁡(t)),\dot{x}(t)=F\left(x(t),a(t)\right), and g:𝒳→𝒴g:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} is an observation map that is not assumed to be injective. Thus, although the underlying state transition is deterministic, only noisy, partial measurements of the state are available. This setting is common in robotics and autonomous driving [9, 65, 66, 67].

To obtain a structured latent dynamics model, we assume the existence of a smooth, possibly nonlinear lifting map Ψ=[ψ1,…,ψN]⊤:𝒳→𝒵⊆ℝN\Psi=[\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{N}]^{\top}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{N}, with N≫nN\gg n, and define the latent representation z=Ψ⁡(x)z=\Psi(x). Here, 𝒵=Ψ⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{Z}=\Psi(\mathcal{X}) is the latent state space, and each ψi:𝒳→ℝ\psi_{i}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} is a scalar observable, i.e., a function of the underlying state, belonging to a common function space ℱ\mathcal{F}, such as a Banach space. The collection {ψ1,…,ψN}\{\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{N}\} forms the dictionary of observables defining the latent variables. For systems with inputs, a Koopman bilinear representation is often more suitable than a purely linear one, as it better captures control-dependent dynamics while retaining computational tractability [62].

Selecting or learning a dictionary of observables that yields an accurate finite-dimensional Koopman state-space model is challenging [68]. Partial observation compounds this challenge because the observables are defined on the underlying state xx, whereas learning relies on noisy, partial measurements and the applied actions [64, 69]. Under partial observation, a finite-dimensional Koopman model generally provides only an approximation of the latent dynamics. The resulting approximation error can be modeled as process noise in the latent transition [70]. Motivated by this viewpoint, we approximate (1) by a hidden Markov model (HMM) with a Koopman bilinear transition (KBT):

𝐳k+1=(𝐈+Δ​t​∑i=0maki​𝔊i)⊤​𝐳k+𝐰k,𝐰k=[0​wk⊤]⊤,wk∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝚺w),\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{k+1}=\big(\mathbf{I}+\Delta t\scriptstyle{\scriptstyle\sum}_{i=0}^{m}a_{k_{i}}\mathfrak{G}_{i}\big)^{\top}\mathbf{z}_{k}+\mathbf{w}_{k},\hskip 8.19447pt\mathbf{w}_{k}=[0\ \ w_{k}^{\top}]^{\top},\hskip 8.19447ptw_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w}), (2a)
and an observation (decoding) model ​yk=h⁡(zk)+vk,vk∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝚺v),\displaystyle\text{and an observation (decoding) model }y_{k}=h(z_{k})+v_{k},\quad v_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v}), (2b)

as illustrated in Fig. 1. Here, the augmented latent state is defined as 𝐳k=[1zk⊤]⊤∈ℝN+1\mathbf{z}_{k}=[1\ \ z_{k}^{\top}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}, which allows the model to capture affine and bilinear control effects in a unified form. The coefficient akia_{k_{i}} denotes the iith element of the augmented action vector 𝐚k=[1ak⊤]⊤∈ℝm+1\mathbf{a}_{k}=[1\ \ a_{k}^{\top}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1}. The matrices 𝔊i=[𝟎𝐕i]\mathfrak{G}_{i}=[\mathbf{0}\ \ \mathbf{V}_{i}] are finite-dimensional approximations of Koopman generators, with the first column fixed at zero. The function h⁡(⋅)h(\cdot) denotes a nonlinear decoder, while 𝚺w\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w} and 𝚺v\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v} are the process and observation noise covariances, respectively. For notational convenience, define the action-dependent matrix approximation of the Koopman operator

𝓚a:=(𝐈+Δ​t​∑i=0maki​𝔊i)=[1𝐛k⊤𝟎𝐀k⊤].\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{K}}^{a}:=\Big(\mathbf{I}+\Delta t\ {\scriptstyle\sum}_{i=0}^{m}a_{k_{i}}\mathfrak{G}_{i}\Big)=\begin{bmatrix}{\scriptstyle 1}&{\scriptstyle\mathbf{b}_{k}^{\top}}\\ {\scriptstyle\mathbf{0}}&{\scriptstyle\mathbf{A}_{k}^{\top}}\end{bmatrix}. (3)

Then the latent KBT in the non-augmented coordinates can be written equivalently as

zk+1=𝐀k​zk+𝐛k+wk.\displaystyle z_{k+1}=\mathbf{A}_{k}z_{k}+\mathbf{b}_{k}+w_{k}. (4)

We model the decoder h⁡(⋅)h(\cdot) as a multilayer perceptron (MLP) parameterized by 𝜻\boldsymbol{\zeta} (hereafter used as h𝜻h_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}), which collects all learnable weights and biases. The initial latent state is assigned a Gaussian prior z0∼𝒩⁡(μ0,𝚺0).z_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}). Accordingly, the HMM in (2) is parameterized by

Θ:={Θ~,𝜻},Θ~:={𝐕0,…,𝐕m,𝚺w,𝚺v,𝚺0,μ0}.\displaystyle\Theta:=\{\widetilde{\Theta},\boldsymbol{\zeta}\},\ \ \widetilde{\Theta}:=\left\{\mathbf{V}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{V}_{m},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0},\mu_{0}\right\}. (5)

Importantly, we do not assume access to the lifting map Ψ\Psi, nor do we explicitly attempt to identify the dictionary of observables. Instead, we posit the HMM in (2) as a structured latent-variable model and estimate the parameter set Θ\Theta by maximizing the likelihood of the observed data. Thus, the learned latent representation is driven by statistical consistency with the observations, rather than by explicit identification of a predefined lifting transformation.

K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} components. K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} has three components parameterized by Θ\Theta:

Representation / inference model: qΘ​(zk∣y≤k,a<k)=𝒩⁡(μk|k,𝚺k|k),\displaystyle q_{\Theta}(z_{k}\mid y_{\leq k},a_{<k})=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k|k},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k|k}), (6a)
Transition model: pΘ​(zk+1∣zk,ak)=𝒩⁡(𝐀k​zk+𝐛k,𝚺w),\displaystyle p_{\Theta}(z_{k+1}\mid z_{k},a_{k})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}_{k}z_{k}+\mathbf{b}_{k},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w}), (6b)
Observation model: pΘ​(yk∣zk)=𝒩⁡(hΘ​(zk),𝚺v).\displaystyle p_{\Theta}(y_{k}\mid z_{k})=\mathcal{N}(h_{\Theta}(z_{k}),\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v}). (6c)

Here, qΘq_{\Theta} is not an independently learned encoder, but an extended Kalman filter (EKF)-induced Gaussian approximation to the filtering posterior obtained from the transition and observation models. Its dependence on Θ\Theta arises through the KBT parameters, the decoder, and the process and observation noise covariances.

2.1 GECM Method for Learning the K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} Parameters

We learn the parameters of K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} from a collection of action–observation trajectories using an iterative expectation-maximization (EM) procedure. Given an observation sequence y0:Ky_{0:K} and the corresponding action sequence a0:K−1a_{0:K-1}, the objective is to maximize the conditional observed-data likelihood pΘ(y0:K∣a0:K−1)p_{\Theta}(y_{0:K}\mid a_{0:K-1}), or equivalently its log likelihood. The pair (z0:K,y0:K)(z_{0:K},y_{0:K}), conditioned on a0:K−1a_{0:K-1}, defines the complete data for the HMM structure. Under the Markov structure of the latent dynamics and the conditional independence of the observations given the latent states, the joint probability density factorizes as

pΘ(z0:K,y0:K∣a0:K−1)\displaystyle p_{\Theta}(z_{0:K},y_{0:K}\mid a_{0:K-1}) =pΘ​(z0)​∏k=0K−1pΘ​(zk+1∣zk,ak)​∏k=0KpΘ​(yk∣zk).\displaystyle=p_{\Theta}(z_{0})\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}p_{\Theta}(z_{k+1}\mid z_{k},a_{k})\prod_{k=0}^{K}p_{\Theta}(y_{k}\mid z_{k}). (7)

For a dataset of RR independent trajectories {y0:K(r),a0:K−1(r)}r=1R,\big\{y_{0:K}^{(r)},a_{0:K-1}^{(r)}\big\}_{r=1}^{R}, the observed-data log likelihood is

ℒ(Θ)=∑r=1RlogpΘ(y0:K(r)|a0:K−1(r))=∑r=1Rlog∫pΘ(z0:K(r),y0:K(r)|a0:K−1(r))dz0:K(r).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\Theta)={\scriptstyle\sum}_{r=1}^{R}\log p_{\Theta}\!\left(y_{0:K}^{(r)}\,\middle|\,a_{0:K-1}^{(r)}\right)={\scriptstyle\sum}_{r=1}^{R}\log\int p_{\Theta}\!\left(z_{0:K}^{(r)},y_{0:K}^{(r)}\,\middle|\,a_{0:K-1}^{(r)}\right)\mathrm{d}z_{0:K}^{(r)}. (8)

Direct maximization of (8) is generally intractable, as the observed-data likelihood requires evaluating the integral over the full latent trajectory in (8) [71, 64], with additional complications arising from the nonlinear observation model. To obtain a tractable training objective, we introduce an auxiliary inference distribution q(r)(z0:K(r))q^{(r)}(z^{(r)}_{0:K}) over latent trajectories. For notational convenience, let Z:=z0:K,Y:=y0:KZ:=z_{0:K},Y:=y_{0:K}, Q:={q(r)}r=1RQ:=\{q^{(r)}\}_{r=1}^{R}, and 𝒜:=a0:K−1\mathscr{A}:=a_{0:K-1}. Then (8) admits the variational decomposition [72, 71]

ℒ(Θ)=ℱ(Θ,Q)+∑r=1R𝒟(q(r)(Z(r))||pΘ(Z(r)∣Y(r),𝒜(r))),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\Theta)=\mathscr{F}(\Theta,Q)+{\scriptstyle\sum}_{r=1}^{R}\mathscr{D}\left(q^{(r)}(Z^{(r)})\ ||\ p_{\Theta}\big(Z^{(r)}\ \mid\ Y^{(r)},\mathscr{A}^{(r)}\big)\right), (9)

where ℱ⁡(Θ,Q)\mathscr{F}(\Theta,Q) is the variational free energy defined as

ℱ(Θ,Q)=∑r=1R𝔼q(r)[logpΘ(Z(r),Y(r)∣𝒜(r))]−𝔼q(r)[logq(r)(Z(r))],\displaystyle\mathscr{F}(\Theta,Q)={\scriptstyle\sum}_{r=1}^{R}\ \ \mathbb{E}_{q^{(r)}}\left[\log p_{\Theta}\big(Z^{(r)},Y^{(r)}\ \mid\ \mathscr{A}^{(r)}\big)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{q^{(r)}}\left[\log q^{(r)}(Z^{(r)})\right], (10)

and 𝒟\mathscr{D} is the non-negative KL divergence between q(r)​(Z(r))q^{(r)}(Z^{(r)}) and pΘ​(Z(r)∣Y(r),𝒜(r))p_{\Theta}\big(Z^{(r)}\ \mid\ Y^{(r)},\mathscr{A}^{(r)}\big). Therefore, ℱ⁡(Θ,Q)\mathscr{F}(\Theta,Q) is the evidence lower bound (ELBO) for the log-likelihood, i.e., ℒ⁡(Θ)≥ℱ⁡(Θ,Q)\mathcal{L}(\Theta)\geq\mathscr{F}(\Theta,Q). Moreover, if the auxiliary distribution coincides with the exact posterior for each trajectory, i.e., q(r)​(Z(r))=pΘ​(Z(r)∣Y(r),𝒜(r)),q^{(r)}(Z^{(r)})=p_{\Theta}\!\left(Z^{(r)}\mid Y^{(r)},\mathscr{A}^{(r)}\right), for all r∈[1:R]r\in[1:R], then the KL term in (9) vanishes and the bound becomes tight, i.e., ℒ⁡(Θ)=ℱ⁡(Θ,Q).\mathcal{L}(\Theta)=\mathscr{F}(\Theta,Q). Starting from an initial parameter Θ0\Theta_{0}, generalized EM approach iteratively updates the auxiliary distribution and model parameters [71]. In the GECM formulation, the M-step is further decomposed into conditional updates over parameter blocks [73]. The steps involved in the GECM procedure are given below:

  • •

    (Expectation) E-step: Update QjQ_{j} such that ℒ⁡(Θj−1)=ℱ⁡(Θj−1,Qj).\mathcal{L}(\Theta_{j-1})=\mathscr{F}(\Theta_{j-1},Q_{j}).

  • •

    (Conditional Maximization) CM-step 1: With 𝜻\boldsymbol{\zeta} fixed at 𝜻j−1\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1}, update Θ~j−1\widetilde{\Theta}_{j-1} to Θ~j\widetilde{\Theta}_{j} such that ℱ⁡({Θ~j,𝜻j−1},Qj)≥ℱ⁡({Θ~j−1,ζj−1},Qj).\mathscr{F}\big(\{\widetilde{\Theta}_{j},\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1}\},Q_{j}\big)\geq\mathscr{F}\big(\{\widetilde{\Theta}_{j-1},\zeta_{j-1}\},Q_{j}\big).

  • •

    (Conditional Maximization) CM-step 2: With Θ~\widetilde{\Theta} fixed at Θ~j\widetilde{\Theta}_{j}, update 𝜻j−1\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1} to 𝜻j\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j} such that ℱ⁡((Θ~j,ζj),Qj)≥ℱ⁡((Θ~j,ζj−1),Qj),\mathscr{F}\big((\widetilde{\Theta}_{j},\zeta_{j}),Q_{j}\big)\geq\mathscr{F}\big((\widetilde{\Theta}_{j},\zeta_{j-1}),Q_{j}\big), and set Θj:=(Θ~j,ζj)\Theta_{j}:=(\widetilde{\Theta}_{j},\zeta_{j}).

Following standard practice for tractable inference computation [74, 51], we employ a Gaussian approximation for latent-state inference and learning. Specifically, for each trajectory rr, we approximate the intractable smoothing posterior pΘ​(Z(r)∣Y(r),𝒜(r))p_{\Theta}(Z^{(r)}\mid Y^{(r)},\mathscr{A}^{(r)}) by a Gaussian inference distribution q(r)​(Z(r))q^{(r)}(Z^{(r)}) computed using an extended Kalman smoother (EKS). The distribution Qj:={qj(r)}r=1RQ_{j}:=\{q_{j}^{(r)}\}_{r=1}^{R} is characterized by smoothing moments computed under the Koopman-bilinear transition model and the nonlinear decoder. The algorithmic version of GECM is highlighted in Alg. 1.

Koopman-consistent initialization for GECM.

Proper initialization of the parameters Θ\Theta, particularly the generator matrices 𝐕i\mathbf{V}_{i}, and the choice of latent dimension are crucial for stable and effective learning. This is especially important in the actuated setting, where the latent transition parameters must capture the action-dependent Koopman-bilinear evolution, whereas the inferred latent states must simultaneously disentangle the effects of the initial condition and the input sequence. As observed in [64], the performance of EM-based learning for actuated Koopman-generator models can be sensitive to initialization, and poor initialization may cause the learning procedure to collapse. This motivates the question of whether the world model can be initialized in a Koopman-consistent manner under partial observation, while also automating the selection of an appropriate latent dimension. We initialize the latent world model using a delay-coordinate Koopman construction. This construction is motivated by Takens’ delay-embedding theorem [75] and the HAVOK framework [76]. Let τ\tau denote the uniform delay-window length, measured in samples. For each trajectory rr, we assume K>τK>\tau, and in practice choose K≫τK\gg\tau so that enough delay windows are available. We define the delay co-ordinates as 𝝃k(r)=[yk(r)yk+1(r)⋯yk+τ−1(r)]⊤\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k}^{(r)}=[y_{k}^{(r)}\ \ y_{k+1}^{(r)}\ \cdots\ \ \ y_{k+\tau-1}^{(r)}]^{\top} and construct the trajectory-wise Hankel matrices 𝐇(r)=[𝝃0(r)𝝃1(r)⋯𝝃K−τ−1(r)],𝐇+(r)=[𝝃1(r)𝝃2(r)⋯𝝃K−τ(r)].\mathbf{H}^{(r)}=\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}^{(r)}\ \ \boldsymbol{\xi}_{1}^{(r)}\ \cdots\ \boldsymbol{\xi}_{K-\tau-1}^{(r)}\right],\ \mathbf{H}_{+}^{(r)}=\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}_{1}^{(r)}\ \ \boldsymbol{\xi}_{2}^{(r)}\ \cdots\ \boldsymbol{\xi}_{K-\tau}^{(r)}\right].

The corresponding Hankel matrices across all trajectories are then given by

𝐇\displaystyle\mathbf{H} =[𝐇(1)𝐇(2)⋯𝐇(R)],𝐇+=[𝐇+(1)𝐇+(2)⋯𝐇+(R)].\displaystyle=\left[\mathbf{H}^{(1)}\ \ \mathbf{H}^{(2)}\ \cdots\ \mathbf{H}^{(R)}\right],\qquad\mathbf{H}_{+}=\left[\mathbf{H}_{+}^{(1)}\ \ \mathbf{H}_{+}^{(2)}\ \cdots\ \mathbf{H}_{+}^{(R)}\right]. (11)

We compute the singular value decomposition (SVD) 𝐇=𝐔𝐒𝐖⊤\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{W}^{\top}, with singular values ordered as σ1≥σ2≥⋯\sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\cdots. We then retain the leading rer_{e} left singular vectors, collected in 𝐔re=[𝒖1,…,𝒖re]\mathbf{U}_{r_{e}}=[\boldsymbol{u}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{u}_{r_{e}}] corresponding to the rer_{e} largest singular values, where rer_{e} is selected as the smallest integer satisfying a prescribed cumulative energy threshold, (OPEN∑i=1reσi2/∑iσi2)≥ρ{\scriptstyle\sum}_{i=1}^{r_{e}}\sigma_{i}^{2}/{\scriptstyle\sum}_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}\big)\geq\rho, with ρ\rho chosen as ρ∈(0.5,1)\rho\in(0.5,1) . For each trajectory rr, the reduced delay coordinates are obtained as

ϕk(r)=𝐔re⊤​𝝃k(r),ϕk+1(r)=𝐔re⊤​𝝃k+1(r).\boldsymbol{\phi}_{k}^{(r)}=\mathbf{U}_{r_{e}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k}^{(r)},\qquad\boldsymbol{\phi}_{k+1}^{(r)}=\mathbf{U}_{r_{e}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k+1}^{(r)}.

Thus, the dimension of the reduced delay representation is determined directly from the Hankel spectrum, rather than selected by manual tuning. We transform the reduced delay coordinates into a finite-dimensional feature vector using separable Legendre polynomial features. For ϕk(r)=[ϕk,1(r),…,ϕk,re(r)]⊤∈ℝre\boldsymbol{\phi}_{k}^{(r)}=[\phi_{k,1}^{(r)},\ldots,\phi_{k,r_{e}}^{(r)}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{e}} and the maximum polynomial degree dpd_{p}, we define the transformed feature

𝐳~k(r)=[1z~k(r)⊤]⊤,z~k(r)=[P1​(ϕk,1(r))​…​Pdp​(ϕk,1(r))​…​P1​(ϕk,re(r))​…​Pdp​(ϕk,re(r))]⊤,\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{k}^{(r)}=\left[1\ \ \widetilde{z}_{k}^{(r)^{\top}}\right]^{\top},\ \widetilde{z}_{k}^{(r)}=\begin{bmatrix}P_{1}(\phi_{k,1}^{(r)})\ \ldots\ P_{d_{p}}(\phi_{k,1}^{(r)})\,\ldots\,P_{1}(\phi_{k,r_{e}}^{(r)})\ \ldots\ P_{d_{p}}(\phi_{k,r_{e}}^{(r)})\end{bmatrix}^{\top}, (12)

where 𝐳~k(r)∈ℝN+1\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{k}^{(r)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}, N=dp​reN=d_{p}r_{e} and Pd​(⋅)P_{d}(\cdot) denotes the Legendre polynomial of degree dd. Each coordinate ϕk,j(r)\phi_{k,j}^{(r)} is independently expanded up to degree dpd_{p}, and the resulting univariate polynomial features are stacked alongside a constant observable. The constant 11 is explicitly included, so the Legendre expansion starts at d=1d=1 to avoid double-counting P0P_{0}. The shifted feature vector 𝐳~k+1(r)\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{k+1}^{(r)} is constructed analogously from ϕk+1(r)\boldsymbol{\phi}_{k+1}^{(r)}. Let R^\widehat{R} denote the number of trajectories used for initialization. Thus, the initialization is performed using only a randomly selected subset of R^\widehat{R} trajectories, rather than all RR trajectories. To preserve the constant observable, we use the previously defined constrained parameterization 𝔊i=[𝟎𝐕i]\mathfrak{G}_{i}=\left[\boldsymbol{0}\ \ \mathbf{V}_{i}\right], so that only the free block 𝐕i\mathbf{V}_{i} is estimated. We initialize the generator matrices by solving

min{𝐕i}i=0m∑r=1R^∑k=0K−τ−1∥z~k+1(r)−z~k(r)Δ​t−[(∑i=0maki(r)𝐕i)⊤𝐳~k(r)]∥22+λg∑i=0m∥𝐕i∥F2,\displaystyle\min_{\{\mathbf{V}_{i}\}_{i=0}^{m}}{\scriptstyle\sum}_{r=1}^{\widehat{R}}{\scriptstyle\sum}_{k=0}^{K-\tau-1}\Big\|\tfrac{\widetilde{z}_{k+1}^{(r)}-\widetilde{z}_{k}^{(r)}}{\Delta t}-\Big[\big({\scriptstyle\sum}_{i=0}^{m}a_{k_{i}}^{(r)}\mathbf{V}_{i}\big)^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{k}^{(r)}\Big]\Big\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{g}{\scriptstyle\sum}_{i=0}^{m}\|\mathbf{V}_{i}\|_{F}^{2}, (13)

where λg>0\lambda_{g}>0 is a small regularization parameter. After obtaining the initialized generator matrices, we compute the one-step prediction residuals on the initialization trajectories. Specifically, for each selected trajectory r=1,…,R^r=1,\ldots,\widehat{R} and valid delay index k=0,…,K−τ−1k=0,\ldots,K-\tau-1, we define z~^k+1(r)=z~k(r)+Δ​t​(∑i=0maki(r)​𝐕i)⊤​𝐳~k(r).\widehat{\widetilde{z}}_{k+1}^{(r)}=\widetilde{z}_{k}^{(r)}+\Delta t\left({\scriptstyle\sum}_{i=0}^{m}a_{k_{i}}^{(r)}\mathbf{V}_{i}\right)^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{k}^{(r)}. The process-noise covariance 𝚺w\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w}, and the initial latent prior (μ0,𝚺0)(\mu_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}) are initialized as

𝚺w=Cov⁡(z~k+1(r)−z~^k+1(r))r,k,μ0=1R^​∑r=1R^z~0(r),𝚺0=Cov⁡(z~0(r))r=1R^.\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w}=\operatorname{Cov}\big(\widetilde{z}_{k+1}^{(r)}-\widehat{\widetilde{z}}_{k+1}^{(r)}\big)_{r,k},\quad\mu_{0}=\tfrac{1}{\widehat{R}}{\scriptstyle\sum}_{r=1}^{\widehat{R}}\widetilde{z}_{0}^{(r)},\quad\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}=\operatorname{Cov}\left(\widetilde{z}_{0}^{(r)}\right)_{r=1}^{\widehat{R}}. (14)

Thus, 𝚺w\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w}, μ0\mu_{0}, and 𝚺0\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} are initialized directly from the residual statistics and initial transformed features induced by the Koopman-consistent initialization.

CM-Step 1.

In CM-step 1 of EM iteration jj, given the inference distribution QjQ_{j} and with 𝜻\boldsymbol{\zeta} fixed at 𝜻j−1\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1}, we update Θ~j−1\widetilde{\Theta}_{j-1} by maximizing the ELBO (10). The required moments under qj(r)q_{j}^{(r)} are denoted by μk(r)=𝔼qj(r)​[zk(r)]\mu_{k}^{(r)}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{j}^{(r)}}\!\big[z_{k}^{(r)}\big], 𝚺k,k(r)=𝔼qj(r)​[(zk(r)−μk(r))​(zk(r)−μk(r))⊤],\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k,k}^{(r)}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{j}^{(r)}}\!\Big[\big(z_{k}^{(r)}-\mu_{k}^{(r)}\big)\big(z_{k}^{(r)}-\mu_{k}^{(r)}\big)^{\top}\Big], and 𝚺k,k+1(r)=𝔼qj(r)​[(zk(r)−μk(r))​(zk+1(r)−μk+1(r))⊤].\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k,k+1}^{(r)}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{j}^{(r)}}\!\Big[\big(z_{k}^{(r)}-\mu_{k}^{(r)}\big)\left(z_{k+1}^{(r)}-\mu_{k+1}^{(r)}\right)^{\top}\Big]. Let

𝐌=∑r=1R∑k=0K−1(𝒂k(r)​𝒂k(r)⊤)⊗ℳk(r), and ​𝐃=∑r=1R∑k=0K−1𝒂k(r)⊤⊗𝒟k(r).\displaystyle\mathbf{M}={\scriptstyle\sum}_{r=1}^{R}{\scriptstyle\sum}_{k=0}^{K-1}\big(\boldsymbol{a}_{k}^{(r)}\boldsymbol{a}_{k}^{(r)\top}\big)\otimes\mathcal{M}_{k}^{(r)},\text{ and }\mathbf{D}={\scriptstyle\sum}_{r=1}^{R}{\scriptstyle\sum}_{k=0}^{K-1}\boldsymbol{a}_{k}^{(r)\top}\otimes\mathcal{D}_{k}^{(r)}. (15)

Now we state the key result for the CM-step 1.

Assumption 1.

The matrices 𝚺w\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w}, 𝚺v\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v}, and 𝚺0\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} remain positive definite, and the training action sequences are persistently exciting (see § F.2).

Proposition 1.

Under Assumption 1, CM-step 1 yields the closed-form ELBO maximizer Θ~j\widetilde{\Theta}_{j} with the decoder parameters 𝛇j−1\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1} held fixed. The complete statement of Proposition 1 and its proof appear in § F.1.1 and § F.1.2, respectively.

Remark 1.

In high-dimensional settings, EM updates can suffer from numerical instability and ill-conditioned estimates [77]. Accordingly, Assumption 1 can be enforced in CM-step 1 by adding small positive regularization terms to the closed-form updates, equivalent to maximizing the regularized ELBO ℱ^​(Θ,Q):=ℱ⁡(Θ,Q)−ℛ⁡(Θ~)\widehat{\mathscr{F}}(\Theta,Q):=\mathscr{F}(\Theta,Q)-\mathscr{R}(\widetilde{\Theta}), where ℛ⁡(Θ~)\mathscr{R}(\widetilde{\Theta}) penalizes ill-conditioned Koopman-bilinear transition parameters and covariance estimates.

CM-Step 2.

In CM-step 2 of EM iteration jj, given QjQ_{j} and with Θ~\widetilde{\Theta} fixed at Θ~j\widetilde{\Theta}_{j}, we update the decoder parameters from 𝜻j−1\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1} to 𝜻j\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j}. We summarize the key result for CM-Step 2 below.

Proposition 2 (Decoder update increases the CM-step objective).

Fix QjQ_{j} and the parameters Θ~j\widetilde{\Theta}_{j}, and define the decoder objective ℒdec​(𝛇):=1R⁡(K+1)​∑r=1R∑k=0K𝔼qj(r)​[‖yk(r)−h𝛇​(zk(r))‖𝚺v,j−12].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dec}}(\boldsymbol{\zeta}):=\tfrac{1}{R(K+1)}{\scriptstyle\sum}_{r=1}^{R}{\scriptstyle\sum}_{k=0}^{K}\ \mathbb{E}_{q_{j}^{(r)}}\Big[\big\|y_{k}^{(r)}-h_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}(z_{k}^{(r)})\big\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v,j}^{-1}}^{2}\Big]. If the decoder parameter update from 𝛇j−1\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1} to 𝛇j\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j} satisfies ℒdec​(𝛇j)≤ℒdec​(𝛇j−1),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dec}}(\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j})\leq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dec}}(\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1}), then ℱ⁡((Θ~j,𝛇j),Qj)≥ℱ⁡((Θ~j,𝛇j−1),Qj).\mathscr{F}\big((\widetilde{\Theta}_{j},\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j}),Q_{j}\big)\geq\mathscr{F}\big((\widetilde{\Theta}_{j},\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1}),Q_{j}\big). Consequently, such an update is a valid generalized CM-step 2 update. We provide the proof in § F.3.

E-Step.

During the E-step of the EM iteration jj, for each trajectory rr, we compute the Gaussian smoothing approximation

qj(r)(Z(r))=𝒩(Z(r);μ0:K(r),𝚺0:K(r))≈pΘj−1(Z(r)∣Y(r),𝒜(r))q_{j}^{(r)}\!\big(Z^{(r)}\big)=\mathcal{N}\!\big(Z^{(r)};\mu_{0:K}^{(r)},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0:K}^{(r)}\big)\approx p_{\Theta_{j-1}}\!\big(Z^{(r)}\mid Y^{(r)},\mathcal{A}^{(r)}\big)

using an EKF followed by a Rauch–Tung–Striebel backward smoother [78, 79]. For brevity, we refer to this procedure as extended Kalman smoothing (EKS). For notational simplicity, we suppress the trajectory index rr below. We now explain the EKF and smoothing process under E-step below.

Forward pass (EKF).

Given the Koopman-bilinear transition (2) and (4), the forward EKF prediction step is given by [80, Section 13.2.3], [78]

μk+1|k=𝐀k,j−1​μk|k+𝒃k,j−1,𝚺k+1|k=𝐀k,j−1​𝚺k|k​𝐀k,j−1⊤+𝚺w,j−1.\displaystyle\mu_{k+1|k}=\mathbf{A}_{k,j-1}\mu_{k|k}+\boldsymbol{b}_{k,j-1},\quad\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1|k}=\mathbf{A}_{k,j-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k|k}\mathbf{A}_{k,j-1}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w,j-1}. (16)

The decoder linearized at the predicted mean: 𝐉k+1,j−1:=∇zh𝜻j−1​(z)|z=μk+1|k.\mathbf{J}_{k+1,j-1}:=\nabla_{z}h_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1}}(z)\big|_{z=\mu_{k+1|k}}. Then the EKF update is given by

𝑺k+1\displaystyle\boldsymbol{S}_{k+1} =𝐉k+1,j−1​𝚺k+1|k​𝐉k+1,j−1⊤+𝚺v,j−1,𝐋k+1=𝚺k+1|k​𝐉k+1,j−1⊤​𝑺k+1−1,\displaystyle=\mathbf{J}_{k+1,j-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1|k}\mathbf{J}_{k+1,j-1}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v,j-1},\quad\mathbf{L}_{k+1}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1|k}\mathbf{J}_{k+1,j-1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{S}_{k+1}^{-1}, (17)
μk+1|k+1\displaystyle\mu_{k+1|k+1} =μk+1|k+𝐋k+1​(yk+1−h𝜻j−1​(μk+1|k)),\displaystyle=\mu_{k+1|k}+\mathbf{L}_{k+1}\big(y_{k+1}-h_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1}}(\mu_{k+1|k})\big), (18)
𝚺k+1|k+1\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1|k+1} =(𝐈−𝐋k+1​𝐉k+1,j−1)​𝚺k+1|k,\displaystyle=\big(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L}_{k+1}\mathbf{J}_{k+1,j-1}\big)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1|k}, (19)

where 𝐋k+1\mathbf{L}_{k+1} is the Kalman gain.

Backward pass (smoothing)

After the forward pass, the backward smoother is initialized by μK=μK|K,𝚺K,K=𝚺K|K.\mu_{K}=\mu_{K|K},\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{K,K}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{K|K}. For k=K−1,…,0k=K-1,\ldots,0, define the smoother gain as 𝐂k=𝚺k|k​𝐀k,j−1⊤​𝚺k+1|k−1.\mathbf{C}_{k}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k|k}\mathbf{A}_{k,j-1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1|k}^{-1}. The smoothed moments are then computed as [78]

μk=μk|k+𝐂k​(μk+1−μk+1|k),𝚺k,k=𝚺k|k+𝐂k​(𝚺k+1,k+1−𝚺k+1|k)​𝐂k⊤.\displaystyle\mu_{k}=\mu_{k|k}+\mathbf{C}_{k}\left(\mu_{k+1}-\mu_{k+1|k}\right),\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k,k}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k|k}+\mathbf{C}_{k}\left(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1,k+1}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1|k}\right)\mathbf{C}_{k}^{\top}. (20)

The lag-one smoothing covariance used in the CM-step is approximated by 𝚺k,k+1=𝐂k​𝚺k+1,k+1\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k,k+1}=\mathbf{C}_{k}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1,k+1}, with 𝚺k+1,k=𝚺k,k+1⊤.\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+1,k}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k,k+1}^{\top}. Thus, for each trajectory, the EKS provides the moments which are used in the subsequent CM-step updates.

3 Uncertainty-aware Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) Control

We use MPPI as a sampling-based receding-horizon controller [81, 82], building on path-integral stochastic optimal control [83]. To make our planning aware of predictive uncertainty, we augment the MPPI roll-out objective with a covariance-dependent risk penalty, in the spirit of risk-aware MPPI variants [84]. After learning K-PWM, we use the learned latent SSM as the dynamics model inside MPPI. At each environment step, the current observation is assimilated using the EKF induced by the learned transition and decoder models, producing a filtering belief (μk|k,𝚺k|k)(\mu_{k|k},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k|k}) initialized from the latent prior (μ0,𝚺0)(\mu_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}). The MPPI scheme then samples SS candidate action sequences around a shifted nominal sequence and rolls out the Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics for a horizon of LL steps from this belief. During each roll-out, the predicted latent mean is decoded to observation space for task-cost evaluation, while the latent covariance is propagated to estimate model uncertainty along the trajectory. Further details on the MPPI scheme and its implementation are provided in appendix G and Alg. 2.

4 Experimental Evaluations

We evaluate the data efficiency of K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} in two sets of experiments focused on prediction and continuous control. In the prediction experiments, we measure prediction accuracy under partial observability and with limited training data on selected Gymnasium MuJoCo systems [85]. In the control experiments, we assess whether models learned from limited data support effective continuous control on high-dimensional tasks built using robot models from MuJoCo Menagerie [86]. To substantiate the data efficiency of K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM}  we limit the training data to 15 (R=15R=15) independently sampled action–observation trajectories per task across all experiments.

Prediction under partial-observation.

We compare the prediction performance of K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} against five prediction-oriented baselines on three partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems (Half Cheetah, Hopper, and Swimmer). The baselines are MTS3 [51], LSTM [42], GRU [43], HiP-RSSM [47], and Ac-RKN [46]. For each system, we independently generate training trajectories by sampling random initial states and applying piecewise-constant random actions within system-specific bounds, with observations corrupted by additive Gaussian measurement noise. To introduce a strict partial observation scenario, we retain 9 of 17 observation components for Half Cheetah, 7 of 11 for Hopper, and 7 of 10 for Swimmer, masking the remaining 8, 4, and 3 components, respectively, in the training data.

Fig. 2 shows the K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} training log-likelihood over GECM iterations. The moving averages plateau near iterations 24, 72, and 62 for Hopper, Swimmer, and Half Cheetah, respectively. The markers indicate the models retained at those iterations. The rise and subsequent plateau in log-likelihood show that GECM improves the fit of K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} to the training data across all three systems. Table 1 shows that K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} achieves the lowest mean RMSE over the prediction horizon THT_{H} for each system. Compared with MTS3, the most accurate baseline, K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} reduces mean RMSE by approximately 38%, 48%, and 66% on Hopper, Swimmer, and Half Cheetah, respectively. K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} also has the shortest training time on each system with a 7.67.6–15.1×15.1\times training speedup over MTS3, and K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} has the shortest training time across all three benchmarks as presented in Fig. 4. Fig. 3 shows mean prediction RMSE as a function of THT_{H}. Across the tested horizons, K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} generally achieves the lowest RMSE, with a clear advantage on Half Cheetah and Swimmer and performance close to MTS3 on Hopper near TH=0.1​sT_{H}=0.1\,\mathrm{s}.

Continuous-control in robotic systems.

We next evaluate the effectiveness of K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} for continuous control of realistic robotic systems when trained on limited data, along with its potential for real-time deployment. We consider four high-dimensional robotic systems from the MuJoCo Menagerie suite: the Franka Emika Panda, TIAGo++, ALOHA 2, and Allegro Hand. We compare against E2C [28], RCE [29], DeepKoopman (DK) [61], and the best-performing prediction-oriented baseline in the preceding experiments (MTS3). For each robot, we independently generate training trajectories by sampling random initial configurations and applying filtered random joint-position commands. We then evaluate the trained models on a circular trajectory-tracking task for each robot, using its end effector (EE) or multiple EEs, as applicable. All methods are evaluated using the presented MPPI scheme with an identical controller configuration, making minor method-specific adaptations where needed to integrate each model. Fig. 5 shows that the training log-likelihood of K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} increases and approaches a plateau on all four robots, with the selected models lying near these plateaus. Fig. 6 reports training times of 6.36.3–22.622.6 minutes for K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM}, making it 1.91.9–5.6×5.6\times faster than MTS3 and faster than DK on every robot, while RCE and E2C train more quickly.

Table 3 reports EE tracking errors over five independent runs. K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} consistently delivers competitive accuracy, ranking among the two most accurate methods on every robot and achieving the lowest mean error on TIAGo++ and Allegro Hand. Table 3 shows that it is also the second-fastest method throughout, providing 1.21.2–2.1×2.1\times speedups over RCE and E2C and 4.34.3–17.0×17.0\times over MTS3. Its mean computation time falls below the 20​ms20\,\mathrm{ms} control period on three robots. On TIAGo++, it remains competitive for real-time control at 22.0​ms22.0\,\mathrm{ms} per step, exceeding the sampling period by only 2.0​ms2.0\,\mathrm{ms}. Although DK is faster, K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} achieves lower mean tracking errors on three robots. Together with its shorter training time than MTS3 and DK, these results demonstrate competitive tracking from limited data with efficient training and online control.

5 Conclusion

We introduced K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM}, a probabilistic world model that couples Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics, nonlinear decoding, and model-induced inference for prediction and control under noisy partial observation. Its structured latent dynamics enable exact propagation of the maintained Gaussian belief through the latent transition and efficient rollouts for uncertainty-aware MPPI control. The proposed GECM procedure combines closed-form conditional updates with gradient-based decoder learning, supported by Koopman-consistent initialization and data-driven latent-dimension selection. Across partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems, K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} achieves lower long-horizon prediction error than the evaluated baselines while substantially reducing training time relative to the strongest prediction baseline. On four high-dimensional MuJoCo Menagerie robots, it delivers competitive tracking accuracy with low per-step computation times, demonstrating potential for real-time deployment. These findings support structured probabilistic latent dynamics as a data- and compute-efficient foundation for prediction and control. Future work will explore richer belief representations, online adaptation, and deployment on physical robots.

Appendix B Supplementary Information for § 1

B.1 Inspiration behind world models.

World models draw inspiration from the internal mental representations that humans and animals use to interpret their surroundings and guide behavior [30, 4]. Fig. 8 illustrates this intuition through imagined actions and their possible consequences: a child anticipates being reprimanded after breaking a vase, while a dog anticipates receiving food after standing on its rear feet. Ha and Schmidhuber [30] develop a computational approach that combines compressed visual representations, a recurrent predictive model, and a controller that uses these representations to select actions. LeCun [4] further emphasizes the role of predictive world models in evaluating possible futures and planning toward objectives.

Fig. 9 illustrates how a world model connects observations to prediction and decision-making. The robot forms an internal representation of its surroundings and predicts how they may evolve under candidate actions. These predictions allow it to evaluate possible outcomes and select actions toward its objective before executing them in the physical environment.

B.2 Pixel-based and vector-based observations.

Pixel-based observations represent visual information as images or video frames. For example, a robot’s camera observation can be written as y⁡(t)=P⁡(t)y(t)=P(t), where P⁡(t)∈ℝm×nP(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is a grayscale image or P⁡(t)∈ℝm×n×3P(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n\times 3} is a color image at time tt. Individual images generally provide only partial information about the underlying environment state [31, 87], as illustrated in Fig. 10.

Vector-based observations consist of numerical sensor readings arranged in a vector. For example, a wheeled robot’s observation may be written as y⁡(t)=[px​(t),py​(t)]⊤∈ℝ2y(t)=[p_{x}(t),p_{y}(t)]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, containing its planar position. This constitutes partial observation of the robot’s pose because its heading, θ⁡(t)\theta(t), is not observed.

Appendix C Discussion and Future Work

K-PWM is motivated by the observation that many physical systems differ from pixel-based world-model benchmarks: measurements are often vector-valued, partially observed, and generated by sensors such as joint encoders, IMUs, or force/torque sensors. In such settings, learning a useful world model requires not only accurate prediction, but also inference over unobserved state variables and calibrated uncertainty propagation over long horizons. By using the learned state-space model itself for latent inference, K-PWM provides a direct connection between prediction, filtering/smoothing, and downstream control.

Our empirical results indicate that Koopman-inspired structure remains valuable even when combined with nonlinear neural decoders. The bilinear latent transition offers a compact control-dependent dynamics model, while the decoder captures nonlinear observation maps. This separation preserves analytical structure in the latent dynamics without restricting the observation model to be linear. The strong prediction performance in low-data regime, suggests that such structure can improve both sample efficiency.

For control, embedding K-PWM inside MPPI provides a direct test of whether the learned belief dynamics are useful beyond open-loop forecasting. The controller uses the inferred belief state and propagates candidate action sequences through the learned model to track task-relevant observation references. Although this is not a full reward-maximizing reinforcement-learning setup, it demonstrates that the learned partially observed world model can support closed-loop planning across robotic tasks with different dynamics. This suggests a path toward control-oriented world models that combine probabilistic inference, structured latent dynamics, and sampling-based planning.

Several directions remain for future work. First, while the present method uses Gaussian approximate inference through EKF/EKS, more expressive inference schemes such as particle filtering, particle smoothing, unscented Kalman filtering, or ensemble-based filtering may better capture multimodal or strongly non-Gaussian posteriors. Second, extending K-PWM from reference-tracking MPPI to reward-driven model-based reinforcement learning would allow direct comparison with policy-learning and latent world-model baselines. Third, online adaptation and uncertainty-aware exploration could further improve robustness when the test environment differs from the training distribution. Finally, deploying K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} on hardware systems with sensor noise, actuator delay, contact uncertainty, and safety constraints would provide an important test of whether structured probabilistic world models can transfer from simulation to real robotic systems.

Appendix D Limitations

Although K-PWM shows strong empirical performance, several limitations remain. First, latent-state inference is based on a Gaussian approximation obtained using an extended Kalman smoother. This approximation is computationally tractable and well matched to the locally linearized decoder, but it may become inaccurate when the posterior is highly non-Gaussian, multimodal, or strongly affected by nonlinear observation ambiguities. Thus, the present formulation is best viewed as an approximate inference method rather than an exact EM procedure.

Second, K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} does not constrain the stability of the learned latent transition. Stability can be important for long horizon predictions, which the GECM procedure doesn’t ensure. Although, regularization helps.

Finally, real robotic systems introduce additional challenges, including unmodeled actuator delays, sensor bias, domain shift, contact uncertainty, and safety constraints during data collection. Extending K-PWM to online adaptation, non-Gaussian filtering, richer uncertainty-aware planning objectives, and hardware experiments is an important direction for future work.

Appendix E Ablations

Effect of structured Koopman initialization.

We evaluate whether the benefit of the structured Koopman initialization comes only from selecting an appropriate latent hidden dimension, or also from providing a useful initialization of the latent dynamics. For both Swimmer and HalfCheetah, we keep the same hidden dimension as that selected by the structured Koopman GECM initialization, but randomly initialize the generator matrices. All other training settings are kept fixed. In both tasks, the randomly initialized models reach the maximum GECM iteration budget without satisfying the convergence criterion. By contrast, the structured Koopman initialization converged in lower GECM iterations. These results indicate that the structured initialization is important not only for model-size selection, but also for placing the Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics in a favorable and well-conditioned region of the parameter space, leading to more stable and substantially faster GECM convergence.

Smaller latent dimensions.

We also evaluate whether K-PWM can be trained with smaller latent dimensions than those selected by the structured Koopman initialization. For HalfCheetah, we train models with smaller latent dimensions using the same training-set size, R=15R=15, and the same optimization settings. In all cases, GECM reaches the maximum iteration budget without satisfying the convergence criterion. By contrast, the latent dimension selected by the structured Koopman initialization leads to successful convergence. This ablation suggests that the proposed initialization is useful not only for parameter initialization, but also for selecting a sufficiently expressive latent dimension for stable EM-based learning under partial observability.

These ablations evaluate convergence stability rather than final prediction accuracy, since the randomly initialized and smaller-dimensional variants did not satisfy the convergence criterion.

GECM versus joint gradient-based training.

To assess the benefit of the GECM procedure in Alg. 1, we train the same K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} model by jointly optimizing all parameters Θ={Θ~,𝜻}\Theta=\{\widetilde{\Theta},\boldsymbol{\zeta}\} with stochastic gradient descent (SGD), instead of alternating the closed-form CM-step 1 updates with the gradient-based decoder update. GECM attains prediction accuracy comparable to joint SGD while training several times faster in wall-clock time. Moreover, GECM avoids the learning-rate tuning and gradient clipping that joint SGD requires for stable training, since the generators, noise covariances, and latent prior are updated in closed form from the smoothed posterior moments.

Bilinear versus linear latent transition.

We next isolate the role of the action-bilinear structure of the KBT in (2). With every component other than the latent transition held fixed, we replace the Koopman-bilinear transition by its linear submodel, in which the action enters the latent dynamics additively rather than multiplicatively. The bilinear transition consistently achieves substantially lower prediction RMSE than its linear counterpart, indicating that the multiplicative action dependence captures control effects that a linear-in-the-action transition cannot.

Model-induced versus amortized inference.

Finally, we evaluate what K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} gains from inferring latent states through the learned model itself. We replace the EKF/EKS inference, which introduces no additional trainable parameters, by a parameter-matched GRU recognition network in the style of DVBF [48] and deep Kalman filters, holding the transition, decoder, latent dimension, training data, and rollout protocol fixed. Replacing the inference mechanism changes the full-window prediction RMSE only marginally, with no consistent winner across tasks and data regimes. Thus, K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} matches the predictive performance of amortized inference without a separately trained recognition network, without KL warm-up, and without an additional inference training budget.

F.2 Supplementary info on Assumption 1

Screening for persistency of excitation (PE).

Consider the action sequence a(r)0:K−1a^{(r)}_{0:K-1} of the rr-th candidate training trajectory. Let a¯i(r)\bar{a}^{(r)}_{i} and si(r)s^{(r)}_{i} denote the sample mean and standard deviation of action component i∈[1:m]i\in[1:m], respectively. Candidates with any si(r)=0s^{(r)}_{i}=0 are rejected before standardization. For the remaining candidates, we define a~k,i(r)=(ak,i(r)−a¯i(r))/si(r)\tilde{a}^{(r)}_{k,i}=(a^{(r)}_{k,i}-\bar{a}^{(r)}_{i})/s^{(r)}_{i} and apply the criterion

λmin​(𝚪(r))≥λPE,𝚪(r):=1K​∑k=0K−1a~k(r)​a~k(r)⊤,\lambda_{\min}\!\big(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{(r)}\big)\geq\lambda_{\mathrm{PE}},\qquad\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{(r)}:=\tfrac{1}{K}{\scriptstyle\sum}_{k=0}^{K-1}\tilde{a}^{(r)}_{k}\,\tilde{a}^{(r)\top}_{k}, (23)

where λPE>0\lambda_{\mathrm{PE}}>0 is a fixed threshold. The test is invariant to nonzero componentwise rescaling of the actions and requires the mean squared projection of the standardized actions onto every unit direction to be at least λPE\lambda_{\mathrm{PE}}. This bound is sufficient for order-one PE of the standardized sequence in the sense of [88]. Whenever a candidate is rejected, we proceed to the next seed.

Ensuring positive definiteness of covariances.

At initialization and after each CM-step 1, we apply eigenvalue floors γv>0\gamma_{v}>0, γw>0\gamma_{w}>0, and γ0>0\gamma_{0}>0 to the observation-noise, process-noise, and initial-state covariance estimates, respectively. For each i∈{v,w,0}i\in\{v,w,0\}, let Ui​diag⁡(λi,1,…,λi,di)​Ui⊤U_{i}\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{i,1},\ldots,\lambda_{i,d_{i}})U_{i}^{\top} be the eigendecomposition of the symmetrized covariance estimate. We set

Σi=Ui​diag​(max⁡{λi,1,γi},…,max⁡{λi,di,γi})​Ui⊤.\Sigma_{i}=U_{i}\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\max\{\lambda_{i,1},\gamma_{i}\},\ldots,\max\{\lambda_{i,d_{i}},\gamma_{i}\}\right)U_{i}^{\top}.

This replaces eigenvalues below γi\gamma_{i} with γi\gamma_{i} and ensures Σi⪰γi​I≻0\Sigma_{i}\succeq\gamma_{i}I\succ 0 throughout training. In exact arithmetic, these positive-definite model covariances yield positive-definite smoothed latent covariances in the EKF–RTS E-step. The corresponding augmented latent second moments are positive definite by the Schur complement.

Generator regularization and conditioning of 𝐌\mathbf{M}.

In CM-step 1 the generator blocks are obtained from the ridge-regularized normal equations

[𝐕0,j⊤𝐕1,j⊤⋯𝐕m,j⊤]=𝐃​(𝐌+γG​𝐈)−1,γG>0,\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{V}_{0,j}^{\top}&\mathbf{V}_{1,j}^{\top}&\cdots&\mathbf{V}_{m,j}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf{D}\,\big(\mathbf{M}+\gamma_{G}\mathbf{I}\big)^{-1},\qquad\gamma_{G}>0,
