Remark 2 (Posterior-mean implementation of CM-step 2).

In implementation, CM-step 2 uses the smoothed posterior means μk|K(r)\mu_{k|K}^{(r)} obtained from the EKF/Rauch smoother as the latent inputs to the MLP decoder. This is a standard tractable choice for nonlinear observation maps, where the exact expectation over the smoothing distribution is not available in closed form. Thus, the decoder block is optimized as a supervised regression problem from smoothed latent representations to observations, while the smoothing covariances are still used in the observation-noise update.

F.4 Why EKS in the E-step?

In the E-step of EM iteration jj, the parameters Θj−1\Theta_{j-1} are fixed and the auxiliary distribution QQ is chosen to maximize the ELBO with respect to QQ. By the standard EM identity,

ℱ⁡(Θj−1,Q)=log⁡pΘj−1​(Y∣𝒜)−DKL​(Q⁡(Z)∥pΘj−1​(Z∣Y,𝒜)),\mathscr{F}(\Theta_{j-1},Q)=\log p_{\Theta_{j-1}}(Y\mid\mathscr{A})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(Q(Z)\,\middle\|\,p_{\Theta_{j-1}}(Z\mid Y,\mathscr{A})\right),

the maximizing choice is

Qj​(Z)=pΘj−1​(Z∣Y,𝒜).Q_{j}(Z)=p_{\Theta_{j-1}}(Z\mid Y,\mathscr{A}).

Thus, the E-step amounts to latent-state smoothing under the current K-PWM parameters.

For each trajectory rr, fixing Θj−1\Theta_{j-1} and the action sequence 𝒜(r)\mathscr{A}^{(r)} gives a linear-Gaussian latent transition model. However, the observation model remains nonlinear through the decoder

yk(r)=h𝜻j−1​(zk(r))+vk(r).y_{k}^{(r)}=h_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1}}(z_{k}^{(r)})+v_{k}^{(r)}.

As a result, the smoothing posterior

pΘj−1​(Z(r)∣Y(r),𝒜(r))p_{\Theta_{j-1}}(Z^{(r)}\mid Y^{(r)},\mathscr{A}^{(r)})

does not generally admit a closed-form Gaussian recursion. We therefore compute the E-step using the Gaussian smoothing distribution induced by the extended Kalman smoother,

qj(r)(Z(r))=𝒩(Z(r);μ0:K(r),𝚺0:K(r)),q_{j}^{(r)}(Z^{(r)})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(Z^{(r)};\mu_{0:K}^{(r)},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0:K}^{(r)}\right),

obtained by locally linearizing the decoder along the filtering and smoothing trajectory. This choice is natural for K-PWM because the subsequent CM-step depends on the latent trajectory only through smoothed first moments, marginal covariances, and lag-one covariances,

μk(r),𝚺k,k(r),𝚺k,k+1(r).\mu_{k}^{(r)},\qquad\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k,k}^{(r)},\qquad\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k,k+1}^{(r)}.

EKS provides exactly these sufficient moments, which are then used to evaluate the expected complete-data log likelihood and update the Koopman-bilinear transition parameters and covariance matrices. Thus, EKS gives a tractable Gaussian E-step that is consistent with the probabilistic state-space structure of K-PWM while accommodating the nonlinear observation decoder. In the special case where h𝜻h_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}} is affine, the model becomes conditionally linear-Gaussian and this smoothing step reduces to the standard Kalman smoother E-step.

F.5 Why Koopman-bilinear form is advantageous ?

We refer the reader to Bruder et al. [62] for a detailed discussion on the advantages of Koopman bilinear representations for controlled nonlinear systems. The Koopman framework makes the dynamics linear with respect to the observables, this linearity does not automatically imply linearity with respect to the control input. Enforcing linear input dependence typically requires restricting the Koopman operator to a subspace of observables containing only linear functions of the input. Finite-dimensional approximations of this restricted operator are then commonly identified from data using EDMD-based linear system identification methods. However, such approximations rely on the implicit assumption that increasing the lifted dimension can recover the true controlled Koopman operator arbitrarily well. This assumption is not valid in general: a valid Koopman representation may fail to exist when the observable space excludes nonlinear functions of the input, even if the state-dependent observable space is infinite-dimensional. Conversely, every controlled system can be represented by a Koopman model with nonlinear input dependence, but such representations are often less useful for control because they sacrifice much of the structure needed for efficient prediction and controller synthesis. Bilinear Koopman models strike a balance between these two extremes by allowing the lifted dynamics to remain linear in the observables while depending multiplicatively on the control input. This structure is particularly natural for control-affine systems, since the continuous-time Koopman generator preserves the control-affine dependence in lifted coordinates, leading to bilinear surrogate dynamics. Consequently, bilinear Koopman realizations are more expressive than linear-input Koopman models, more structurally compatible with general controlled nonlinear systems, and more computationally tractable than fully nonlinear-input realizations. This makes them especially attractive for model-based control, where one seeks predictive flexibility without losing the algorithmic benefits of structured lifted dynamics.

Appendix G Supplementary Information for § 3

We use model predictive path integral (MPPI) control as a sampling-based receding-horizon controller to evaluate whether the learned K-PWM model supports downstream control under partial observability. At each environment time step kk, the controller maintains a latent belief (μk,𝚺k)(\mu_{k},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k}), obtained from the EKF using the most recent partial observation. Starting from this belief, MPPI samples SS candidate action sequences over an LL-step planning horizon,

ak:k+L−1(s)=𝒫𝒜(ak:k+L−1base+ϵk:k+L−1(s)),s=1,…,S,a_{k:k+L-1}^{(s)}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\left(a_{k:k+L-1}^{\mathrm{base}}+\epsilon_{k:k+L-1}^{(s)}\right),\qquad s=1,\ldots,S,

where ak:k+L−1basea_{k:k+L-1}^{\mathrm{base}} is a base sequence constructed from the current nominal sequence and, when available, reference or gait-prior actions. The term ϵk:k+L−1(s)\epsilon_{k:k+L-1}^{(s)} denotes temporally correlated Gaussian exploration noise, and 𝒫𝒜\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}} denotes projection onto the admissible action set 𝒜\mathcal{A}, implemented as componentwise clipping to the environment action bounds in our experiments.

For each sampled action sequence, the controller samples an initial latent state from the current belief,

z¯k(s)∼𝒩⁡(μk,𝚺k),\bar{z}_{k}^{(s)}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k}),

and rolls out the learned Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics,

z¯k+l+1(s)=𝐀k+lz¯k+l(s)+𝒃k+l,l=0,…,L−1.\bar{z}_{k+l+1}^{(s)}=\mathbf{A}_{k+l}\bar{z}_{k+l}^{(s)}+\boldsymbol{b}_{k+l},\qquad l=0,\ldots,L-1.

The predicted observations are obtained through the learned decoder,

y^k+l+1(s)=h𝜻​(z¯k+l+1(s)).\hat{y}_{k+l+1}^{(s)}=h_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}\!\left(\bar{z}_{k+l+1}^{(s)}\right).

Each rollout is assigned the cumulative discounted cost

J(s)=∑l=0L−1γl​ℓMPPI​(y^k+l+1(s),yk+l+1ref,ak+l(s),ak+l−1(s),𝚺k+lroll),J^{(s)}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\gamma^{l}\ell_{\mathrm{MPPI}}\!\left(\hat{y}_{k+l+1}^{(s)},y_{k+l+1}^{\mathrm{ref}},a_{k+l}^{(s)},a_{k+l-1}^{(s)},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+l}^{\mathrm{roll}}\right),

where γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1] is the discount factor. The MPPI stage cost ℓMPPI\ell_{\mathrm{MPPI}} contains task-dependent observation-reference tracking terms, control effort, action smoothness, and an uncertainty penalty. In particular, the uncertainty term is

ℓunc=λunc​tr​(𝚺k+lroll),\ell_{\mathrm{unc}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{unc}}\,\mathrm{tr}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+l}^{\mathrm{roll}}\right),

where the rollout covariance is propagated using the nominal Koopman transition,

𝚺k+l+1roll=𝐀k+lbase​𝚺k+lroll​(𝐀k+lbase)⊤+𝚺w.\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+l+1}^{\mathrm{roll}}=\mathbf{A}_{k+l}^{\mathrm{base}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+l}^{\mathrm{roll}}\left(\mathbf{A}_{k+l}^{\mathrm{base}}\right)^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w}.

Since 𝚺roll\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{roll}} is propagated along the base sequence, it is the same for all candidates: the uncertainty term measures the latent uncertainty of the nominal plan over the horizon and adds a common offset to every J(s)J^{(s)}, which the cost normalization below removes. The candidate weights are therefore determined by the remaining terms of ℓMPPI\ell_{\mathrm{MPPI}} (tracking, control effort and, where used, action smoothness), while the uncertainty term is part of the reported planning cost.

After evaluating all sampled rollouts, the costs are normalized as

J~(s)=J(s)−mini⁡J(i)stdi​(J(i))+ε,s=1,…,S.\widetilde{J}^{(s)}=\frac{J^{(s)}-\min_{i}J^{(i)}}{\mathrm{std}_{i}(J^{(i)})+\varepsilon},\qquad s=1,\ldots,S.

The normalized costs define exponential MPPI weights,

w(s)=exp(−J~(s)/λ)∑i=1Sexp(−J~(i)/λ),s=1,…,S,w^{(s)}=\frac{\exp\!\left(-\widetilde{J}^{(s)}/\lambda\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{S}\exp\!\left(-\widetilde{J}^{(i)}/\lambda\right)},\qquad s=1,\ldots,S,

where λ>0\lambda>0 is the MPPI temperature. The nominal action sequence is then updated by the weighted average

a¯k:k+L−1+=∑s=1Sw(s)ak:k+L−1(s).\bar{a}_{k:k+L-1}^{+}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}w^{(s)}a_{k:k+L-1}^{(s)}.

Only the first action ak=a¯k+a_{k}=\bar{a}_{k}^{+} is applied to the true MuJoCo environment. The optimized sequence is shifted forward by one step, appended with a terminal nominal action, and reused as the nominal sequence at the next control step.

Appendix H Supplementary Material for § 4

Computing Resources

All experiments were run on a laptop with an Intel Core i7-11850H CPU, 32 GB RAM, and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Laptop GPU with 16 GB VRAM.

Systems considered in experiment.

As already mentioned in the main text, we consider two sets of systems based-on Gymnasium MuJoCo 11 1 https://gymnasium.farama.org/environments/mujoco/ and DeepMind’s MuJoCo Menagerie22 2 https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/stable/models.html as shown in Fig. 11.

H.1 Training Data Collection

For every task we simulate a pool of 150150 trajectories of actions and observations. The candidate trajectory rr of the system ss uses the seed s+rs+r, which fixes its random input sequence, its initial state, and its measurement noise. Before simulation, the input sequence is tested for PE condition (23) with λPE=0.02\lambda_{\mathrm{PE}}=0.02. A candidate action sequence that fails the PE test, or whose rollout is invalid (e.g., a fall for Hopper, any contact for the free-space robots), is discarded and the next seed is used until 150150 trajectories are accepted. Every observation channel is corrupted at every time step by independent Gaussian noise νk∼𝒩⁡(0,σo2)\nu_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}_{o}), and all models are trained on the noisy observations. For each system, we draw disjoint training, validation, and test sets of 15, 10, and 10 trajectories, respectively, from the pool of 150 candidate trajectories. These drawn trajectories are held fixed for all the methods. In the next, Δ​t\Delta t represent sampling time.

Gymnasium tasks.

Half Cheetah, Hopper and Swimmer (Gymnasium v5), started from Gymnasium’s seeded reset. Actions are piecewise-constant torques, each drawn uniformly from [−a¯,a¯][-\bar{a},\bar{a}] and held for a fixed interval: Half Cheetah (a¯=1\bar{a}=1, held 11 s, for 1212 s at Δ​t=0.1\Delta t=0.1 s), Swimmer (a¯=1\bar{a}=1, held 0.20.2 s, for 66 s at Δ​t=0.1\Delta t=0.1 s) and Hopper (a¯=0.1,0.1,0.3\bar{a}=0.1,0.1,0.3 for thigh, leg and foot; held 66 ms; for 0.30.3 s at Δ​t=2\Delta t=2 ms; as larger torques make the Hopper fall). We use σo=0.01\sigma_{o}=0.01 for Half Cheetah and Swimmer, and σo=0.001\sigma_{o}=0.001 for Hopper. The partial observation setting for the Gymnasium systems considered is provided in Table 5. The actions with time for the training trajectories are shown in Fig. 12.

MuJoCo Menagerie tasks.

We simulate each robot with a time step of Δ​t=0.02\Delta t=0.02,s. Trajectories last 66 s for Panda and 33 s for the other robots. We sample initial configurations uniformly from the middle 40%40\% of the joint range for Panda and TIAGo++ and from the middle 60%60\% of the actuator range for ALOHA 2 and Allegro. The actions are joint-position commands. We sample a new target a⋆a^{\star} uniformly every 0.30.3 s for Panda and every 0.060.06 s for the other robots. For Panda and TIAGo++, we restrict the targets to 60%60\% of the actuator range. For ALOHA 2 and Allegro, we use the full range. At each time step, we move the command toward the current target using the first-order filter ak+1=ak+α⁡(a⋆−ak)a_{k+1}=a_{k}+\alpha(a^{\star}-a_{k}), with α=0.1\alpha=0.1 for Panda and α=0.2\alpha=0.2 for the other robots. We observe joint angles, joint velocities, and the Cartesian positions of the end effectors or fingertips. The resulting observation dimensions are ny=17n_{y}=17, 3434, 3030, and 4444 for Panda, TIAGo++, ALOHA 2, and Allegro, respectively. We discard trajectories in which any contact occurs and set the observation noise level to σo=0.005\sigma_{o}=0.005. The actions with time for the training trajectories are shown in Fig. 13.

H.2 Experiment Setting

Exclusion of Otto et al. [64] baseline.

We attempted to evaluate Otto et al. [64], the closest partially observed Koopman baseline, on the MuJoCo Menagerie tasks. We used the same training data and latent dimensions selected for K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM}, while retaining the random generator initialization prescribed in [64]. In these experiments, the EM iterations failed to converge, producing non-finite generator estimates or degenerate covariance matrices that prevented subsequent inference and control evaluation. A possible contributing factor is the interaction between random initialization and the affine observation model: the latent dynamics must accommodate observation structure that K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} can represent through its nonlinear decoder, potentially increasing sensitivity to the initial latent representation and the conditioning of the EM updates. However, the observed failures do not establish a unique cause or imply that the method cannot converge under alternative configurations. We therefore omit this baseline from the reported Menagerie comparison and interpret these results as a numerical limitation of the tested configuration.

Initialization of GECM parameters.

For the Koopman-consistent initialization of the K​-​PWM\mathrm{K\text{-}PWM} parameters we use the same procedure and hyperparameters for both task families: R^=10\hat{R}=10 randomly selected training trajectories, a delay window of τ=10\tau=10 samples, Legendre features of maximum degree dp=3d_{p}=3 and generator ridge λg=10−6\lambda_{g}=10^{-6}; the observation-noise covariance is initialized as 𝚺v=0.01​𝐈\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v}=0.01\,\mathbf{I}. The latent dimension N=dp​reN=d_{p}\,r_{e} follows from the Hankel spectrum through the energy threshold ρ\rho, which is the only task-specific initialization parameter: for the Gymnasium tasks ρ=0.8\rho=0.8 (HalfCheetah), 0.950.95 (Hopper) and 0.70.7 (Swimmer), giving N=9N=9, 66 and 99; for the Menagerie robots ρ=0.6\rho=0.6 (Franka Emika Panda, Allegro Hand), 0.990.99 (TIAGo++) and 0.70.7 (ALOHA 2), giving N=15N=15, 3636, 234234 and 1818. The MLP decoder has input dimension NN, one hidden layer of width 2​N2N with ReLU activations, and output dimension nyn_{y}; its parameters 𝜻\boldsymbol{\zeta} use the default PyTorch initialization for linear layers.

During GECM training.

During GECM the closed-form updates are regularized by a generator ridge γG\gamma_{G} and eigenvalue floors γw,γv,γ0\gamma_{w},\gamma_{v},\gamma_{0} on 𝚺w,𝚺v,𝚺0\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}: γG=10−2\gamma_{G}=10^{-2} for HalfCheetah, 10−410^{-4} for TIAGo++, 10−610^{-6} for Allegro Hand and 10−310^{-3} otherwise, with γw=γv=γ0=10−6\gamma_{w}=\gamma_{v}=\gamma_{0}=10^{-6} for Panda and Allegro Hand and 10−510^{-5} otherwise. Each decoder update (CM-step 2) runs 10001000 Adam epochs at learning rate 10−210^{-2}. In CM-step 2 of GECM iteration jj, starting from 𝜻j−1\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j-1}, the decoder is fitted to the pairs (μk(r),yk(r))(\mu_{k}^{(r)},y_{k}^{(r)}) of smoothed latent means and observations, k=0,…,Kk=0,\ldots,K, r=1,…,Rr=1,\ldots,R, by minimizing the mean-squared reconstruction error with full-batch Adam for 10001000 epochs at learning rate 10−210^{-2} (decayed by a factor of 0.99990.9999 every 100100 epochs), on a random 80%80\% of the pairs; the remaining 20%20\% are only monitored.

GECM training convergence and stopping criteria.

After each GECM iteration jj, we evaluate the regularized training log-likelihood per observed scalar,

ℓj=ℒ⁡(Θj)−ℛ⁡(Θ~j)R⁡(K+1)​ny,\ell_{j}=\frac{\mathcal{L}(\Theta_{j})-\mathscr{R}(\widetilde{\Theta}_{j})}{R\,(K+1)\,n_{y}},

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is the observed-data log-likelihood (8) of the RR training trajectories and ℛ\mathscr{R} is the regularizer of the regularized ELBO. Iteration jj becomes the incumbent, and its parameters Θj\Theta_{j} are stored, only if ℓj>ℓ⋆+ϵ\ell_{j}>\ell^{\star}+\epsilon, where ℓ⋆\ell^{\star} is the value of the current incumbent and ϵ=10−3\epsilon=10^{-3} nats. Training is considered converged, and stops, once 1010 consecutive iterations fail to improve on the incumbent by more than ϵ\epsilon (Patience P=10P=10); this rule is applied only after a minimum of 2020 iterations, and training is capped at jmax=200j_{\mathrm{max}}=200. The incumbent parameters are returned.

MPPI Implementation.

For the Menagerie robots, the observation stacks the joint angles q∈ℝnqq\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{q}}, the joint velocities q˙∈ℝnq\dot{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{q}} and the Cartesian positions pe∈ℝ3p_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} of the nen_{e} tracked end effectors (fingertips for the Allegro Hand), y=[q⊤q˙⊤p1⊤⋯pne⊤]⊤y=[\,q^{\top}\ \ \dot{q}^{\top}\ \ p_{1}^{\top}\cdots p_{n_{e}}^{\top}\,]^{\top}. For candidate ss at horizon step ll, the decoded prediction y^k+l+1(s)=[q^⊤q˙^⊤p^1⊤⋯p^ne⊤]⊤\hat{y}_{k+l+1}^{(s)}=[\,\hat{q}^{\top}\ \ \hat{\dot{q}}^{\top}\ \ \hat{p}_{1}^{\top}\cdots\hat{p}_{n_{e}}^{\top}\,]^{\top} is compared with the reference yk+l+1refy_{k+l+1}^{\mathrm{ref}} through the stage cost

ℓMPPI=\displaystyle\ell_{\mathrm{MPPI}}={} λee​∑e=1ne‖p^e−peref‖22+λqnq​‖q^−qref‖22+λq˙nq​‖q˙^−q˙ref‖22\displaystyle\lambda_{\mathrm{ee}}{\textstyle\sum}_{e=1}^{n_{e}}\big\|\hat{p}_{e}-p_{e}^{\mathrm{ref}}\big\|_{2}^{2}+\tfrac{\lambda_{q}}{n_{q}}\big\|\hat{q}-q^{\mathrm{ref}}\big\|_{2}^{2}+\tfrac{\lambda_{\dot{q}}}{n_{q}}\big\|\hat{\dot{q}}-\dot{q}^{\mathrm{ref}}\big\|_{2}^{2}
+λa​‖ak+l(s)‖22+λunc​tr​(𝚺k+l+1roll),\displaystyle+\lambda_{a}\big\|a_{k+l}^{(s)}\big\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{unc}}\,\mathrm{tr}\!\big(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+l+1}^{\mathrm{roll}}\big),

with λee=800\lambda_{\mathrm{ee}}=800, λq=20\lambda_{q}=20, λq˙=2\lambda_{\dot{q}}=2, λa=0.01\lambda_{a}=0.01 and λunc=0.001\lambda_{\mathrm{unc}}=0.001. The end-effector term carries the tracking task; the joint terms keep the robot near the reference configuration, which the end-effector positions alone do not determine for redundant arms; the control term penalizes large commands; and the uncertainty term penalizes the latent covariance propagated along the rollout, 𝚺kroll=𝚺k\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k}^{\mathrm{roll}}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k} and 𝚺k+l+1roll=𝐀k+lbase​𝚺k+lroll​(𝐀k+lbase)⊤+𝚺w\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+l+1}^{\mathrm{roll}}=\mathbf{A}_{k+l}^{\mathrm{base}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k+l}^{\mathrm{roll}}(\mathbf{A}_{k+l}^{\mathrm{base}})^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w}, with 𝐀k+lbase\mathbf{A}_{k+l}^{\mathrm{base}} the Koopman-bilinear transition under the base action ak+lbasea_{k+l}^{\mathrm{base}}. The rollout cost is J(s)=∑l=0L−1γl​ℓMPPIJ^{(s)}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\gamma^{l}\ell_{\mathrm{MPPI}} with γ=0.98\gamma=0.98, and a non-finite cost is replaced by a large constant before normalization. The base sequence is abasek:k+L−1=0.85arefk:k+L−1+0.15a¯k:k+L−1a^{\mathrm{base}}_{k:k+L-1}=0.85\,a^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k:k+L-1}+0.15\,\bar{a}_{k:k+L-1}, clipped to the actuator range, where a¯\bar{a} is the shifted nominal sequence; the exploration noise follows ϵl=0.85​ϵl−1+0.15​ηl\epsilon_{l}=0.85\,\epsilon_{l-1}+0.15\,\eta_{l} with ηl∼𝒩⁡(0,0.152​𝐈)\eta_{l}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.15^{2}\mathbf{I}); and the action appended after the shift is ak+Lrefa^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k+L}. The cost weights, base sequence and exploration noise are identical for every world model. MPPI uses S=2000S=2000 candidates, a horizon of L=20L=20 steps (0.40.4 s at Δ​t=0.02\Delta t=0.02 s) and temperature λ=0.7\lambda=0.7. The actions are joint-position commands (nq=7n_{q}=7, 1414, 1212 and 1616 for Panda, TIAGo++, ALOHA 2 and Allegro Hand), and the robots track ne=1n_{e}=1, 22, 22 and 44 end effectors, respectively. Each closed-loop run tracks a 5.585.58 s circular reference (279279 control steps), starting from the home configuration with every joint offset by 𝒰⁡[−0.01,0.01]\mathcal{U}[-0.01,0.01] rad; the controller observes all channels corrupted by zero-mean Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.0050.005, while tracking errors are measured on the noise-free state. Results are reported over five runs (seeds 00–44), each seed fixing the start offset, the measurement noise and the MPPI sampling; all world models see the same seeds.

RMSE metric.

For each prediction horizon, RMSE is computed per test trajectory and then summarized across trajectories. Specifically, for prediction horizon ss, let y^i,s∈ℝny\widehat{y}_{i,s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{y}} and yi,s∈ℝnyy_{i,s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{y}} denote the predicted and true observations for test trajectory ii. The per-trajectory RMSE is

RMSEi​(s)=1ny​∑d=1ny(y^i,s,d−yi,s,d)2.\mathrm{RMSE}_{i}(s)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{y}}\sum_{d=1}^{n_{y}}\left(\widehat{y}_{i,s,d}-y_{i,s,d}\right)^{2}}.

The reported RMSE is the mean over the NtestN_{\mathrm{test}} test trajectories,

RMSE¯​(s)=1Ntest​∑i=1NtestRMSEi​(s),\overline{\mathrm{RMSE}}(s)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{test}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{test}}}\mathrm{RMSE}_{i}(s),

and the reported standard deviation is the sample standard deviation across test trajectories,

Std⁡(s)=1Ntest−1​∑i=1Ntest(RMSEi​(s)−RMSE¯​(s))2.\mathrm{Std}(s)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{test}}-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{test}}}\left(\mathrm{RMSE}_{i}(s)-\overline{\mathrm{RMSE}}(s)\right)^{2}}.

Thus, the uncertainty reported with RMSE reflects variability across test trajectories rather than the standard error of the mean.

End-effector tracking RMSE.

For each robot, we evaluate end-effector position tracking against the reference trajectory using the noise-free simulated positions. Let ErE_{r} denote the end-effector tracking RMSE, expressed in millimeters, for independent run rr. Table 2 reports the mean and sample standard deviation over Nrun=5N_{\mathrm{run}}=5 runs:

E¯=1Nrun​∑r=1NrunEr,sE=1Nrun−1​∑r=1Nrun(Er−E¯)2.\bar{E}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{run}}}\sum_{r=1}^{N_{\mathrm{run}}}E_{r},\qquad s_{E}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{run}}-1}\sum_{r=1}^{N_{\mathrm{run}}}(E_{r}-\bar{E})^{2}}.

Thus, the reported values are E¯±sE\bar{E}\pm s_{E}, with the standard deviation measuring variability across independent runs. Joint-angle and joint-velocity errors are excluded from this metric.
